<reason>Both sides were sharp, but B built and sustained the cleaner decisive comparison. B's opening set two burdens — the stake/loss test and the substitution problem — and pressed both relentlessly. The substitution line ("classify it as gambling and the same skin appears at £15; the animation dies, the wallet is identical") forced A into an awkward posture: A embraced the substitution as its "victory," and then had to call the £15 fixed-price purchase "ordinary commerce," which B mined twice to argue A's motion licenses the actual spending harm. B also successfully turned A's answer to the Pokémon analogy: once A relied on speed, lighting, one-tap access and dynamic odds, B could say A had abandoned its own category test ("money in, chance out, variable prize") and conceded that intensity, not category, is doing the work — which is B's ground. A's best moments were real: the anti-avoidance turn in closing (dust conversion is itself a sham designed to keep the child spinning) and the "bounded by wanting vs bounded by nothing" distinction, plus the strong pressure question about how spend caps for minors work without age assurance. But B answered that squarely with the age-signalling vs document-grade verification distinction, which A only got to rebut with a clipped final line. A also incurred four clipping penalties, including on its closing, while B stayed within limits throughout. A never made the obvious available move — that gambling classification and general spending regulation are not mutually exclusive — leaving B's "only one of us reaches the bill" frame largely unanswered.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's turn on the substitution concession [B2.3]/[B4.5]: A had called the fixed-price outcome "the victory," and B converted that into "your own win condition is a world where the child spends the identical £60 on the identical pixels, now declared harmless — a reclassification, not a rescue." A's "bounded by wanting" reply was principled but never fully neutralized it.</best_rebuttal>
